name: Urdu alphabet (Nastaliq)
signature: Right-to-left words descend diagonally in calligraphic Nastaliq, with dense joins and carefully placed dots.
combination: Letters join right-to-left and change shape by position. Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq; the bundled Naskh font is currently a readable fallback while the course data records Nastaliq structure. Short vowels are normally omitted.
notes: Starter inventory for the first Urdu shared-spine lessons, grounded in Zer o Zabar. This canonical script-data file keeps Noto Naskh as its readable path-checking fallback; the book and Language Ladder presentation use the separately vendored Noto Nastaliq Urdu family. The full letter inventory remains explicit next-track work.

Naskh folds both forms more sharply than Nastaliq. This learner path covers the independent form and fits the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback. strokeOrder: shape the three close teeth from right to left
flow directly into the final bowl without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Sīn, shīn, baṛī he, nūn, and nūn-e ġhunna, independent س calligraphic and handwriting animations and Sīn instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The independent-form animations and adjacent prose show one uninterrupted stroke: shape the three close teeth from right to left, then flow directly into the final bowl without lifting. components: three close teeth and final bowl
two lower dots and one centered upper dot
strokeOrder: shape the three close teeth from right to left
flow directly into the final bowl without lifting
after one lift, place the lower-left dot
after another lift, place the lower-right dot
after a third lift, place the centered upper dot

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Sīn, shīn, baṛī he, nūn, and nūn-e ġhunna, independent ش calligraphic and handwriting animations and Shīn instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The independent-form animations draw the full standard toothed sīn body first in one uninterrupted stroke, then place the lower-left dot, the lower-right dot, and finally the centered upper dot: four strokes separated by three pen lifts. The lesson arranges the dots as two below with one nestled between them above. As with sīn, an optional long gentle curve may replace the teeth, especially in handwriting, while the three dots stay centered over either form. This learner path covers the standard toothed independent form and fits the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

components: main-line stem, flatter bowl, and final hook
strokeOrder: draw the independent stem downward
flow right to left through the flatter bowl and finish with the pronounced hook without lifting
after one lift, draw the long slash down from the upper right toward the stem

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Be, kāf, and short vowels, independent ک calligraphic and handwriting animations and Kāf instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations and the adjacent prose show two separate pen strokes. First draw the stem as part of the main line, continuing right to left through the flatter bowl and pronounced final hook without lifting. Then lift once, return to the upper right, and draw the long downward slash toward the stem; the lesson explicitly says not to write kāf in one penstroke. Final and independent kāf are often flatter than be and have a more pronounced hook at the end. This learner path fits that order to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu uses ک rather than Arabic ك, is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

letters.notes: Urdu uses this kaf shape rather than Arabic ك.

strokeOrder: draw the tall independent upright downward
continue below the baseline through the leftward bowl and back up without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Pe, gāf, alif, and lām, independent ل calligraphic and handwriting animations and Lām instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations show one uninterrupted stroke: begin at the top, descend the tall upright, continue below the baseline through the leftward bowl, and turn back up its outer side without lifting. The adjacent prose identifies lām as a connector and separately calls out the below-baseline bowl in the final form. This learner path covers the independent form and fits the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

strokeOrder: shape the round head
continue down the tail below the baseline without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Te, mīm, jīm, che, and more diacritics, independent م calligraphic and handwriting animations and Mīm instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations keep the round head and descending tail in one uninterrupted stroke. The lesson says calligraphic and handwritten mīm look different: an ordinary constant-width pen typically draws the handwritten head as a counterclockwise loop, while the tail of independent or final mīm drops below the baseline. This learner path fits the same head-to-tail, zero-lift order to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

strokeOrder: sweep the independent bowl from right to left below the baseline
after one lift, place the dot near the baseline

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Sīn, shīn, baṛī he, nūn, and nūn-e ġhunna, independent ن calligraphic and handwriting animations and Nūn instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations draw the bowl first in one uninterrupted right-to-left run, then lift once and place the dot near the baseline. The lesson says final and independent nūn use a bowl extending below the baseline with the dot near the baseline itself; initial and medial nūn instead resemble a be-series tooth with one dot above it. This learner path covers the independent form and fits the two-stroke order to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

strokeOrder: start at the independent form's upper right
curve down and left around the base, then return up the right side and cross the top without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Chhoṭī he, do-chashmī he, chhoṭī ye, baṛī ye, and punctuation, independent ہ calligraphic and handwriting animations and Chhoṭī he instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations draw one uninterrupted counterclockwise loop: start at the upper right, curve down and left around the base, then return up the right side and cross at the top without lifting. The lesson describes the independent form as an oval or teardrop. Initial and medial chhoṭī he instead dip to a small divot with a number-6-like mark below, which is occasionally omitted medially; the final form is a small curve or squiggle that goes up and then down. This learner path covers the independent form and fits the continuous zero-lift order to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

strokeOrder: start at the independent form's upper right and descend through the S curve
continue left around the below-baseline bowl and finish at its rising tip without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Chhoṭī he, do-chashmī he, chhoṭī ye, baṛī ye, and punctuation, independent ی calligraphic and handwriting animations and Chhoṭī ye instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations draw one uninterrupted dotless S-shaped body: start at the upper right, descend through the upper curve, then sweep left around the below-baseline bowl and finish at its rising tip without lifting. The lesson says independent and final chhoṭī ye use this S-shaped form and make an ī sound. Initial and medial ye instead resemble a be-series tooth with two dots below the line and can represent chhoṭī or baṛī ye; those dots do not belong to the independent form. This learner path covers independent chhoṭī ye and fits the continuous zero-lift order to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

strokeOrder: sweep the independent dotless bowl from right to left below the baseline without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Sīn, shīn, baṛī he, nūn, and nūn-e ġhunna, independent ں calligraphic and handwriting animations and Nasalization with nūn-e ġhunna instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations draw one uninterrupted right-to-left bowl below the baseline without lifting. The lesson explicitly says final and independent nūn-e ġhunna look like nūn without any dot; initial and medial forms instead look identical to regular nūn and may occasionally carry a sukūn or small semicircular diacritic. The vendored Noto Naskh U+06BA outline exactly matches the U+0646 nūn body contour with the dot removed, so this learner path reuses that verified bowl motion while preserving the positional distinction. Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

letters.notes: Nūn-e ġhunna marks a nasal vowel; its final and independent forms lack the dot of ن.

strokeOrder: descend from the independent form's upper right and sweep left across the broad bowl
curl back underneath at the far left
continue right along the lower fold without lifting

strokeOrderSource.citation: Zer o Zabar, Chhoṭī he, do-chashmī he, chhoṭī ye, baṛī ye, and punctuation, independent ے calligraphic and handwriting animations and Baṛī ye instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026)
strokeOrderSource.variation: Both independent-form animations draw one uninterrupted folded bowl: start at the upper right, descend and sweep left across the upper edge, curl back underneath at the far left, then continue right along the lower fold without lifting. The lesson says independent and final baṛī ye represents e, ai, and y and folds backward underneath the preceding letters. Initial and medial ye instead use the be-series tooth with two dots below and can represent either chhoṭī or baṛī ye. This learner path covers independent baṛī ye and fits the continuous zero-lift motion to the course's vendored Noto Naskh fallback; Urdu is conventionally printed in Nastaliq, and the app's true Nastaliq face remains separate from this canonical script-data fallback.

letters.notes: Baṛī ye usually occurs at the end of a word; its independent and final forms are dotless.
